title: Improving Pop-Up Debates: Better Prompts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. diagnoses why some of his classroom pop-up debates failed and traces the problem to the prompt rather than the students. He borrows Les Lynn's five criteria for a good debatable question: openness, balance, focus, authenticity and intellectual interest. For each one he offers a bad prompt from his own past and a repaired or good one, such as narrowing the Mongols question to the effects of Mongolian conquest. He also makes a pedagogical point that interest can be built, since content knowledge gained through study is what makes a debate such as the Cold War lively. He closes with March Madness as a model prompt that meets all five criteria. The post is a practical prompt-design framework for history and humanities teachers.
points: Most failed pop-up debates can be traced to the prompt; Lynn's five criteria (open, balanced, focused, authentic, interesting) work as a pre-flight check.
Focus fails when a key term is ambiguous: 'How barbaric were the Mongols?' splits on two definitions, so asking about mostly positive or negative effects of Mongol rule fixes it.
A quick authenticity test is to Google the prompt; if nothing comes up, nobody argues about it and the debate will be yawny.
Interest can be built through knowledge-rich study, so a prompt that excites only history nerds in September can excite everyone after a unit on the Cold War.
Balance depends on the evidence supplied as well as the wording, and one-sided sources can ruin an otherwise balanced question.
quotes: I've held more than a few pop-up debates that went badly, and I could trace the badness back to before the debate started. What am I talking about? The Plague of the Poorly Formulated Pop-Up Debate Prompt.
Well, true — but then it wouldn't be Romeo and Juliet either. If arguing one of the sides requires such drastic measures, it's not defensible to the degree we want it to be for a good pop-up debate.

But the trouble is that it can quickly get off track based on how we define “barbaric.” On the one hand, if we're defining barbaric as “savagely cruel and exceedingly brutal,” as Google's first definition does, then this is really a question of comparing the severity of their actions to those of contemporary societies.

If you can Google your debatable prompt and absolutely nothing comes up, that might be a sign that almost no one on the planet really argues about what you are prompting. As I recall, this debate was a bit yawny — authenticity is one of the reasons why.

If I were to tell my students at the start of the year that we'd be having a big debate about who was most responsible for the Cold War, the USA or the USSR, only the history nerds would be excited. But by the time we finish studying the Cold War, kids are into the pop-up debate because they know a lot about the topic.
